title_ar: شرح ورقات إمام الحرمين في أصول الفقه -الشريط الثاني
title_en: Commentary on the Waraqat of Imam al-Haramayn on Legal Theory — Tape Two
body_ar: أقسام العلم عقد هذا الباب لبيان تقسيمات العلم وتعريف أقسامه بعد أن عرف العلم وما يقابله وهو الجهل ، فقال العلم الضروري وهو ما لا يقع عن نظر واستدلال كالعلم الواقع بإحدى الحواس الخمس ، فقسم العلم هنا إلى ضروري ونظري ، فالضروري منسوب إلى الضرورة بمعنى الذي يضطر الإنسان إليه ، فالإنسان مضطر لأن يعرفه بذاته ، قال والعلم الضروري ما لا يقع عن نظر واستدلال ، أي ما يحصل دون نظر واستدلال لا يتوقف على نظر ، والنظر كما قلنا هو الفكر ، واستدلال والاستدلال هو إقامة الدليل ، فالضروري هو ما لا يحتاج إلى التأمل لا يحتاج إلى حركة النفس فيه لا بنظر أي تفكر ولا باستدلال فالعلم الواقع بإحدى الحواس الخمس فالمرئيات والمسموعات والمشمومات والملموسات كلها يحصل بها العلم الضروري فلا يحتاج الإنسان فيها إلى تأمل ، فمن سمع كلام إنسان جزم بأنه متكلم ، لأن هذا الكلام صدر منه ، ومن رآه يفعل فعلا جزم بذلك دون أن يحتاج إلى تأمل في هذا أو إقامة دليل عليه وهكذا .
body_en: The divisions of knowledge. This chapter is set down to set out the divisions of knowledge and to define its categories, after knowledge and its opposite — which is ignorance — have been defined. He said: necessary knowledge (al-ʿilm al-ḍarūrī), which is that which does not arise from reflection (naẓar) and inference (istidlāl), such as the knowledge that comes about through one of the five senses. So he divided knowledge here into the necessary and the reflective (naẓarī). "Necessary" is derived from necessity (ḍarūrah), in the sense of that to which a person is compelled: a person is compelled to know it of itself. He said: necessary knowledge is that which does not arise from reflection and inference — that is, what is obtained without reflection and inference, what does not depend on reflection. And reflection (naẓar), as we said, is thought (fikr). And inference — istidlāl is the setting up of the evidence (iqāmat al-dalīl). So the necessary is that which needs no deliberation, which needs no movement of the soul within it, neither by reflection — that is, thinking — nor by inference. As for the knowledge that comes about through one of the five senses: things seen, things heard, things smelled and things touched — necessary knowledge is obtained by all of them, so a person needs no deliberation in them. Whoever hears the speech of a person concludes with certainty that he is a speaker, because this speech issued from him; and whoever sees him perform an act concludes that with certainty without needing to deliberate over it or to set up evidence for it, and so on.

flags.note: ḍarūrah here is the epistemic modality of al-Waraqat's opening chapter, NOT the legal threshold of necessity carried in glossary.json ('a technical threshold, not general hardship'). The glossary rendering must not be applied to this passage. Same caution as the kalām exemption in style guide section 8: the term attaches to a proposition, not to an act.

translator_notes: The Waraqat of Imam al-Haramayn al-Juwayni is the standard elementary primer of legal theory; the Sheikh is commenting on its chapter on the divisions of knowledge. The pronoun 'he said' throughout refers to al-Juwayni as author of the base text, not to the Sheikh.
No legal ruling is given anywhere in this text. It is epistemology preliminary to legal theory, so none of the five-rulings vocabulary applies.
